decision_rationale: All three domain agents maintain Pause after deliberation, though with lower confidence (PM: 72%→65%, Data: 82%→80%, Marketing: 70%→62%). The Risk/Critic recommends Roll Back (68% confidence) citing KI-001 data-loss exposure. The strongest argument against Pause is the Risk/Critic's point that ~130,000 users remain exposed to a data-loss bug with no confirmed fix — this is a valid concern. However, the agents' revised positions converge on a conditional Pause with a hard 48h gate on KI-001: if the fix is not shipped in 48h, the decision escalates to Roll Back. This conditional approach preserves the 28.5% adoption signal and avoids the brand cost of a full rollback, while setting a firm deadline that addresses the Risk/Critic's core concern. The deliberation shifted all agents to treat KI-001 as the #1 priority — above the opt-out toggle and expansion planning.

critique.rationale: All three agents recommend Pause, but I challenge their shared assumption that the recovery trend is sufficient to hold at 25%. KI-001 (draft data loss) remains in 'investigating' status after 10 days — this is a critical severity bug reported by 3 users and amplified on Reddit. At 25% rollout (130,000 users exposed), the blast radius for a data-loss bug is unacceptable. The PM's focus on funnel completion (28.5%) is an anchoring bias — strong adoption means MORE users are exposed to the data-loss risk. The Data Analyst notes 3 of 9 metrics still breach thresholds but still recommends Pause; this conflates 'improving' with 'acceptable'. The Marketing agent correctly identifies the amplification risk but underweights it — a single viral thread about data loss can do more brand damage than all the performance complaints combined. Cancellations averaged 34/day over 10 days vs 10/day baseline — a 3.4x increase. The recovery trend is only 3 days old and untested at higher rollout. I recommend Roll Back to protect user trust while fixes are shipped.

critique.dissent_notes: The majority leans toward Pause, but pausing at 25% still exposes ~130k users to a data-loss bug (KI-001) with no confirmed fix. The draft-disappearing bug alone warrants rollback — it is a trust-destroying event and 3 users have already reported it. If even 0.1% of the 130k cohort experiences data loss, that's 130 affected users with high churn and social amplification risk.

revised_verdicts.rationale: After reviewing the Risk/Critic's challenge, I acknowledge the KI-001 data-loss concern is more urgent than my initial framing suggested. The 28.5% funnel adoption IS a double-edged sword — high engagement means more users exposed to the bug. However, I maintain Pause over Roll Back: the Day 7 hotfix shows the engineering team can ship targeted fixes, and rolling back would lose the adoption signal and create user confusion. My confidence is lower (65% vs 72%) because the D7 retention decline (39.2% vs 42.0% target) combined with the unresolved KI-001 makes the risk profile worse than I initially weighted. I now prioritise KI-001 fix as the #1 gate — above the opt-out toggle.

The critique that 'improving ≠ acceptable' is fair — I've slightly lowered my confidence to 80%. The 3 breaching metrics (crash rate, D7 retention, support tickets) need more time to confirm sustained recovery. I agree with the PM that KI-001 should be the #1 gate.

revised_verdicts.rationale: The Risk/Critic's emphasis on the Reddit data-loss PSA and its amplification potential has shifted my assessment. I underweighted the brand damage of a viral data-loss thread — it IS more damaging than performance complaints. However, I still favour Pause over Roll Back because: (1) rolling back generates its own negative narrative ('they had to pull the feature'), (2) the accessibility user (#35) represents a powerful positive story we'd lose, and (3) transparent acknowledgement of the issue can convert critics into advocates if we fix fast. My confidence has dropped from 70% to 62% — if KI-001 is not fixed within 48h, I would shift to Roll Back to protect the brand.
